item.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
item.description:
Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access

When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

item.title: The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same | Gordon Brown
item.description:
As Spain heads into a critical election, polling shows that many voters attracted by rightwing parties don’t really agree with their ideas

When Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France, Poland, Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism.

Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states. Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east, Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south.

item.title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
item.description:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.
